key_finding: Shrouding the exact-minimum autopay option cut minimum-only credit card payments by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce debt, and reduced autopay enrollment enough to increase missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment on credit card autopay defaults with a six-month follow-up window (NBER working paper).
why_it_matters: Shows a default/nudge can shift nominal sign-up behavior substantially while leaving the underlying financial outcome unchanged or worse, directly supporting the support team's concern that enrolment numbers can be a vanity metric for round-ups.
limitations: credit-card debt paydown, not a savings product
no measure of persistence beyond 6 months
liquidity constraints identified as the mechanism, may not generalize to all round-up users
relevance_reason: Directly tests whether a default/nudge changes actual financial behavior versus just nominal enrollment status, the core trade-off the brief asks about.

key_finding: Synthesizes evidence that automatic enrollment and default investment options raise short-term retirement plan participation but can produce longer-term disengagement, with plan-design remedies like auto-escalation and re-enrollment reviewed.
methodology: Narrative literature overview of defined-contribution plan design research; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a synthesized effect-size backdrop for defaults and disengagement in the closest large analogous literature, useful context though not directly transferable to the app decision.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement setting, not a self-directed consumer app
no primary consumer financial product data
abstract gives no numeric effect sizes
relevance_reason: Closest large review of default-driven participation and disengagement, useful background even though its setting is employer retirement plans.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term retirement participation but induces long-term passivity—low contribution rates, inactive account management, and account churn—undermining welfare gains from participation alone.
methodology: Narrative policy analysis of US default-enrollment retirement literature; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly voices the support team's objection that participation-rate gains from defaults can mask passive, disengaged, low-value enrollees.
limitations: US employer retirement plans, not a liquid consumer product
no primary data or effect sizes in abstract
recommendations are pension-specific
relevance_reason: States the counter-argument to defaults-always-help directly, matching the brief's stated concern about passive enrollees.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for downstream default effects, identifying time course of choice, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as moderators of whether default effects persist or backfire.
methodology: Conceptual review and framework synthesis of consumer default-effect literature; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to predict when a round-up default will persist versus produce quick disengagement, directly informing what to measure post-launch at 6-12 months.
limitations: theoretical/conceptual, not new empirical data
not specific to financial products
no effect sizes given
relevance_reason: Directly addresses persistence and downstream consequences of default choice architecture in consumer settings, the central open question in the brief.

key_finding: Default assignment in Medicare Part D produces large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity to the default is extremely insensitive even when the default causes substantial losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default plan options among Medicare Part D low-income beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Shows default persistence is not conditional on the default being good for the individual, cautioning that opt-out enrollment could keep low-value round-up users passively locked in rather than actively benefiting.
limitations: healthcare/insurance domain, not consumer financial savings
government-administered default rather than app-based
no measure of amount saved
relevance_reason: Strongest evidence that default persistence is not conditional on the default being good for the person, bearing on the distributional/manipulation-risk question.

key_finding: Steady-state saving rates rise by only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation once turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and opt-outs are accounted for; only 40% of auto-escalated employees stay on schedule at the first escalation date.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans' administrative data incorporating employee turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the counter-argument: measured default effects on enrollment substantially overstate real long-run savings impact once attrition and opt-out are included.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-administered rather than self-directed app
does not address active choice or manipulation perception
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving with a quantified estimate, satisfying the brief's request for contradicting evidence.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income pension savers raised participation by 23 percentage points, but most enrollees actively opted back out, and the default effect was strongest when incentives were high, options complex, and opting out difficult.
methodology: Natural experiment using linked administrative and survey data around a nationwide auto-enrollment policy introduction.
why_it_matters: Names the exact conditions under which a default enrollment effect is weak—low incentive, simple choice, easy opt-out—which describes the round-up feature closely, predicting a much smaller enrollment lift than typical pension defaults.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, not a consumer banking app
government-administered rather than self-directed digital product
no data on amount saved or long-run persistence
relevance_reason: Names the moderating conditions (low stakes, simple choice, easy exit) that predict how large our round-up default effect will actually be, a direct transfer to the brief's decision.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, with modest savings increases at the longer horizon though inequality in savings is reduced; a life-cycle model estimates a $250 switching cost.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel comparing 12-month and 36-month outcomes, with a structural life-cycle model.
why_it_matters: Best quantified evidence that default-driven enrollment gains shrink substantially at medium-run horizons, directly bearing on whether the round-up feature's enrollment lift would persist at 6-12 months.
limitations: retirement plan setting rather than liquid consumer savings
switching costs estimated for pension context may not transfer to a low-friction app toggle
no employer-vs-app comparison offered
relevance_reason: Best quantified evidence on persistence/attenuation of default effects over time, the exact horizon the brief asks about.

key_finding: Across experiments including a five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes, but applying (or refusing) a default lowers the client's rating of the advisor's advice, mediated by perceived honesty, and framing of the default question shifts the chosen allocation.
methodology: Series of controlled experiments, including a large representative five-country European sample, on default and framing effects in financial risk-allocation decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly measures when a default reads as manipulative in a consumer financial EU context and shows framing effects on the chosen level, bearing on both the entry-design manipulation risk and the multiplier anchoring question.
limitations: wealth-management advisory context rather than a banking app round-up feature
single risk-allocation decision, no long-term persistence data
no direct opt-in/opt-out enrollment comparison
relevance_reason: EU consumer financial experiment quantifying both anchoring on default framing and perceived manipulation risk, matching two of the brief's key open questions directly.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment lifted participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants passively accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still anchored to both defaults after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans tracking participation and default retention over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that people anchor on whatever contribution level is pre-set, the historical result the multiplier-level decision is measured against.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, not a self-directed consumer banking app
does not address the 'employer as trusted intermediary' difference the brief flags
older data predating app-based fintech and current regulatory climate
relevance_reason: The classic anchoring-on-default-level result that the level-design decision is being tested against.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out effort cost; adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20-25-30% menu captures 69% of achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on large-scale transactional tipping data plus an independent stated-preference survey identifying true preferences.
why_it_matters: Quantifies how much preset-menu adherence is friction rather than preference and shows how adjusting the menu of preset options trades welfare against revenue—directly analogous to choosing which round-up multiplier to preset and whether to add options.
limitations: tipping decisions, not savings behavior
single transactional context (taxi payment), not a banking app
welfare/revenue tradeoff numbers are domain-specific to tipping norms
relevance_reason: Provides a rigorous, transferable method for decomposing default adherence into preference vs. friction and quantifying menu-design welfare tradeoffs, directly bearing on the preset-multiplier decision.

key_finding: Only up to 0.7% of eligible UK employees ever activated an opt-in short-term savings account, but among those who did, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution after 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a payroll-deduction short-term savings account rollout at five UK firms, tracking activation rates and 12-month account status.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the opt-in trade-off for a liquid, withdraw-anytime short-term savings product like round-ups: very low uptake but strong 12-month persistence among those who opt in, informing whether pure opt-in could work without a default.
limitations: employer-administered payroll deduction, not a self-directed banking app feature
UK firm employees, not general consumer app users
no comparison against an opt-out or active-choice arm
relevance_reason: Closest available evidence on enrollment and 12-month persistence for a liquid short-term savings product under an opt-in design, the same entry mechanism the brief is deciding between.

key_finding: Characterizes when opt-out-minimizing versus opt-out-maximizing defaults are asymptotically optimal, showing that weighted opt-out minimization is the general optimum when designer and chooser values align, with extensions for externalities, fees, and normative disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical characterization of optimal default policy validated by numerical simulations.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative framework for judging whether defaulting users into round-ups is welfare-improving versus manipulative depending on whether the firm's and users' interests align, relevant to the reputational/dark-pattern risk question.
limitations: purely theoretical, no empirical population or product studied
assumes a specifiable designer objective, unclear for a bank's incentives
no consumer financial or app-specific application given
relevance_reason: Provides the normative economic theory needed to judge when an opt-out default is welfare-justified versus manipulative, bearing on the brief's manipulation-risk concern.

key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from dark-pattern manipulation under EU law.
methodology: Doctrinal/legal analysis mapping EU dark-pattern regulation; abstract-only for the taxonomy's structure.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU-law framework for judging whether a pre-checked opt-out or pre-set multiplier crosses from a helpful default into a regulated dark pattern — directly informs which entry and level designs are legally and reputationally defensible.
limitations: legal/doctrinal analysis, not empirical evidence of behavioral effect
no effect sizes or outcome data
relevance_reason: Provides the EU regulatory lens the brief explicitly asks for on when a default reads as helpful versus manipulative, bearing directly on entry-design reputational risk.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees remained at the default 12 months post-hire versus roughly half staying at lower defaults, and low-income employees were disproportionately anchored at a likely-suboptimal rate.
methodology: Field study of an employer retirement plan's high default contribution rate compared against a literature review of lower-default plans; abstract-only for underlying data.
why_it_matters: Shows a higher pre-set default anchors a substantial minority long after enrollment and anchors lower-income people more strongly — a direct caution for which round-up multiplier to pre-select.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer product
employer match structure creates incentives absent in a bank app
relevance_reason: Closest prior evidence on whether a pre-set contribution level anchors people below what they might otherwise choose, bearing on the multiplier decision.

key_finding: Abstract text is unavailable (record appears corrupted/garbled), so no extractable finding on payroll savings automation experiments can be reported.
methodology: abstract-only; content missing/corrupted in the record provided.
why_it_matters: Title suggests UK field experiments automating short-term (non-retirement) payroll savings, which would be a close analog to round-up savings defaults, but no usable content is available to assess impact or effect size.
limitations: abstract text missing/garbled, cannot verify claims or effect sizes
unclear whether outcomes concern short-term liquid savings or retirement savings
relevance_reason: Title indicates a close analog to consumer short-term savings automation, but the record provides no usable abstract content to score properly.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17–19% and arranged overdraft charges 4–8%, an estimated £170–240 million in annual market-wide savings, yet consumers still capture less than half of the potential savings available.
methodology: Large-scale field experiments (automatic enrollment vs. control) run at major UK banks, with market-wide extrapolation.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world evidence of opt-out-style enrollment into a bank feature producing measurable financial benefit at scale, while showing defaults alone leave substantial value unrealized — directly relevant to whether opt-out enrollment into round-up savings changes real outcomes, not just nominal sign-up.
limitations: overdraft alerts are a notification mechanism, not a savings sweep
no data on contribution-level anchoring
relevance_reason: Same setting as the brief — consumer bank app, opt-out enrollment into a financial feature — with real behavioral and monetary outcomes, the strongest direct precedent available.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment raises savings, but each additional month enrolled also raises unsecured debt by about £7 and mortgage balances by £118, partially offsetting the savings gain, while modestly lowering defaults and raising credit scores.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment: randomized roll-out of UK automatic pension enrollment across ~160,000 small employers, tracked over 41 months.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that defaulting people into saving is a costless win by showing offsetting borrowing behavior — exactly the net-welfare check the brief wants before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: employer-mediated pension context, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
debt-offset mechanism may not transfer to small round-up sums
relevance_reason: Strong contradicting evidence that automatic enrollment defaults can produce offsetting harm, relevant to the support team's disengagement/harm concern.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment ordeal (an extra step) to health insurance auto-enrollment reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying the removal of an auto-enrollment policy in a health insurance selection market.
why_it_matters: Shows that friction removed from (or added to) enrollment produces large, demographically uneven effects — direct evidence on who is helped or hurt by enrollment friction, relevant to the brief's distributional concern about opt-in versus opt-out.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not consumer savings
adverse selection dynamics specific to insurance markets don't map directly onto a savings feature
relevance_reason: Rigorous causal estimate of how enrollment friction reshapes who is enrolled, informing the distributional question the brief raises about who a default helps or hurts.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, default-inexperienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across U.S. political campaign websites that added pre-checked recurring-donation boxes at different times.
why_it_matters: A directly analogous real-money default (a pre-checked recurring financial commitment) that both lifts nominal sign-up and generates a refund/complaint pattern mirroring the support team's fear about passively-enrolled, unhappy users, while showing the default changed how money flowed without people compensating on amount.
limitations: political donations, not a savings/banking product
no 6-12 month persistence data beyond the donation window
relevance_reason: Closest quantified evidence of a pre-checked financial default causing both large uptake and measurable buyer's-remorse/refund harm, directly bearing on the dark-pattern and disengagement risk the brief asks about.

key_finding: In a search-with-default-option experiment, the presence of a default raises reservation utility via a reference effect, and people who reject the default disproportionately find higher-ranked alternatives, with both effects present in the data.
methodology: Lab experiments testing a reference-dependent search model with a default option; abstract-only for effect magnitude.
why_it_matters: Offers a theoretical mechanism for why defaults can bias people away from actively searching for a better option, background theory relevant to why a pre-set multiplier might anchor even capable users.
limitations: general economic search experiment, not a financial-product or enrollment setting
no numeric effect sizes reported in the abstract
relevance_reason: Provides a general behavioral-economics mechanism for default-driven anchoring, background theory rather than direct evidence for the round-up decision.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects still evident 15 months after rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the staggered EU DMA choice-screen rollout across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether forced active choice can durably shift users away from a pre-set default at scale in an EU regulatory context — exactly the active-choice-vs-default comparison the brief needs for the entry decision, showing persistence well beyond onboarding.
limitations: mobile browser default, not a financial/savings product
no data on amount saved or contribution levels
relevance_reason: Best available large-scale, EU-regulation-driven evidence on whether active choice produces durable behavior change relative to defaults, central to the entry-design decision.

key_finding: A 'generalizable active choice' interface, letting one opt-out choice apply to a broader set of choices, reduced disruption (98% of participants felt undisrupted in the best scheme, a 40-point improvement over baseline) with only a slight loss in opt-out utility, in a 410-participant usability study.
methodology: Usability study (n=410) comparing nine opt-out interface schemes in a browser extension implementing Global Privacy Control.
why_it_matters: Named method transfer: the generalizable-choice UI principle — letting one input apply across a larger decision set with minimal disruption — is directly reusable for designing a low-friction active-choice onboarding screen for the round-up feature that avoids feeling like a forced ordeal.
limitations: privacy opt-out context, not a financial product
measures disruption/comprehension, not enrollment or savings outcomes
relevance_reason: Named method transfer: the low-disruption active-choice interface design tested here is directly applicable to building a non-punitive forced-choice onboarding flow.

key_finding: Opt-out defaults increased sign-up for effortful tasks (exam registration), but gains in actual completion and success appeared only for individuals already predisposed to respond, with no effect on target outcomes for non-responsive individuals despite higher sign-up.
methodology: Two field experiments changing university exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out, tracking sign-up, participation, and pass rates.
why_it_matters: Named mechanism transfer: direct evidence that opt-out defaults inflate nominal sign-up without changing real effortful behavior for people not already inclined to engage — precisely the support team's concern that passively-enrolled round-up users will not actually save, and shows the effect is concentrated in a subgroup rather than universal.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a financial product
no data on withdrawal or amount saved
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the assumption that default-driven enrollment translates into real behavior change, with the same responsive/non-responsive heterogeneity structure the brief asks about.

key_finding: After target-date funds became the default investment option under the Pension Protection Act, younger and older workers' stock allocations diverged along the TDF glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel of millions of U.S. retirement investors, 2006–2018, exploiting the PPA default-option policy change.
why_it_matters: Suggests defaults can reshape allocation choices strongly while leaving contribution levels largely unmoved — a caution that a pre-set round-up multiplier might not shift savings rates as much as hoped, though this evidence concerns investment mix rather than savings rate.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement account setting
concerns portfolio allocation rather than the enrollment/contribution-rate decisions central to the brief
relevance_reason: Weak but relevant employer-analogy evidence that default options can fail to move contribution levels even while reshaping other choices, bearing indirectly on anchoring.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, all tested nudges, including default options, significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings in China, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative and default-option nudges, and effects varying by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey (n=220) testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: Direct contradicting evidence that a default option can backfire and reduce contribution willingness rather than raise it, undercutting the 'defaults always help' premise the brief explicitly asks to test, in an individually self-directed (not employer-mandated) savings decision.
limitations: small sample (n=220) online survey rather than a real product
Chinese cultural/institutional context may not generalize to EU consumer banking
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the shortlist: shows default options can reduce rather than increase voluntary savings willingness, directly answering the brief's request for evidence against the 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people rated financial nudges positively overall, preferred System-2 (deliberative) framings and savings-framed interventions, and transparency did not reduce approval.
methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment, 36 hypothetical financial-intervention vignettes, representative Australian sample (n=2,100), varying transparency, framing and System-1/2 targeting.
why_it_matters: Tells us which framing of the round-up feature (savings-framed, deliberative System-2 style) is least likely to be perceived as manipulative, directly informing how we present opt-out or active-choice enrolment to avoid a dark-pattern read.
limitations: Hypothetical vignette survey, not actual product behaviour
Australian sample, not EU regulatory context
No enrolment or persistence data, only stated attitudes
relevance_reason: Directly measures consumer approval/manipulation-perception of financial nudges, the exact reputational-risk question the brief raises about opt-out defaults.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a bank-account payment channel instead of cash produced no average increase in savings, but raised balances specifically among people who had zero savings beforehand.
methodology: Field experiment/randomized offer of bank-account payment channel to conditional cash transfer beneficiaries; tracks savings and downstream asset/trust outcomes.
why_it_matters: Suggests channel/default changes mainly help the already-non-saving segment rather than lifting savings broadly, a heterogeneity finding relevant to who a round-up default actually helps.
limitations: Population is CCT beneficiaries in a developing-country welfare context, not app users choosing a savings feature
About payment channel choice, not enrolment defaults per se
No multi-year persistence data reported
relevance_reason: Bears on whether channel/account defaults change real savings amounts versus just nominal participation, and shows effects concentrated in a specific subgroup.

key_finding: An automatic IRA with an emergency-savings (liquid) component is compared against alternative designs on contribution levels and liquid-fund availability, though the retrieved abstract text is fragmentary.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to be a policy/simulation comparison of automatic IRA designs with liquid emergency-savings features.
why_it_matters: Touches the liquidity dimension the brief flags as different from locked pensions, potentially informing whether a liquid, withdrawable default behaves like locked retirement defaults.
limitations: Abstract is truncated/fragmentary, so no usable effect sizes are available
Government/IRA policy setting, not a bank app feature
Unclear methodology
relevance_reason: Nominally addresses a liquid, automatic-enrolment savings vehicle, the closest analogy to a round-up feature among the retirement literature, but evidence is too thin to lean on.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and most automatically-enrolled employees stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation that almost no opt-in employee had chosen voluntarily.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment at a single large U.S. corporation comparing 401(k) elections under opt-in versus automatic-enrollment regimes.
why_it_matters: The original demonstration that a default is read as implicit advice, not just adopted passively, which is the mechanism behind the anchoring risk the brief worries about for the 1x/2x/5x multiplier.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plan, so the 'trusted intermediary' mechanism does not transfer as the brief notes
Single firm, pre-2001 setting, predates app-based liquid savings
No dark-pattern/manipulation framing considered
relevance_reason: Foundational classic study the later default-effect and anchoring literature responds to; establishes the core 'default as implicit advice' mechanism relevant to the multiplier decision.

key_finding: Abstract unavailable; the paper reportedly compares savings behaviours between automatic and voluntary enrollment in a defined-contribution retirement plan.
methodology: abstract-only, no details available.
why_it_matters: Could add another automatic-vs-voluntary enrollment comparison, but without the abstract there is nothing concrete to weigh against the current design decision.
limitations: No abstract text available, so no effect sizes or methodology can be assessed
Employer defined-contribution plan setting, not a consumer app
relevance_reason: Title matches the brief's core enrolment-design question but the record carries no usable content.

key_finding: Limited trust in financial institutions and minority/non-national status were both associated with under-saving and with early withdrawal of retirement savings after a pension-freedom reform in Estonia.
methodology: Analysis of three nationally representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a policy reform introducing an early-withdrawal option to a mandatory pension scheme.
why_it_matters: Identifies which users are most likely to disengage or withdraw prematurely from a savings product, directly relevant to the support team's worry that passively-enrolled users withdraw within weeks and to who a round-up default would end up hurting.
limitations: Mandatory pension scheme rather than a consumer round-up feature
Correlational survey design, not a randomized default manipulation
Estonian institutional/trust context may not generalise to the EU app's user base
relevance_reason: Directly speaks to the brief's distributional concern about who is helped versus hurt by enrolment and who withdraws, via institutional trust and minority-status heterogeneity.

key_finding: Across a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrollment vaccination policy reduced stated behavioral intentions and policy approval rather than increasing them.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment (G7 countries) manipulating reflection on a default-enrollment nudge for COVID-19 boosters.
why_it_matters: Shows that making a default's mechanics salient can backfire and reduce buy-in, a caution for any transparency/disclosure requirement layered onto an opt-out round-up default under EU consumer-protection rules.
limitations: Health/vaccination policy domain, not financial services
Hypothetical policy vignette, not actual enrolment behaviour
No financial-product or app-level outcome measured
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults are cost-free once disclosed; reflection on a default reduced support and intended uptake, relevant to how transparently we disclose the opt-out mechanism.

key_finding: Among U.S. Millennials, automatic enrollment and employer matching were both associated with higher retirement-plan participation, while their absence and poor communication explained most non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study, controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance and assets.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the standard employer-plan finding that automatic enrollment lifts participation, but adds little beyond more rigorous experimental work already reviewed for this brief's consumer setting.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plan with employer matching, the exact intermediary mechanism the brief says does not transfer
Observational/correlational, not causal
No amount-saved, persistence, or anchoring data
relevance_reason: Additional confirmatory evidence for the default-enrollment effect in the (excluded) employer-plan setting; useful only as background, not decision-changing.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations in Denmark, automatic (passive) employer contributions raised real wealth accumulation, while subsidies requiring active choice mostly just shifted assets between accounts; each $1 of subsidy raised total saving by only about 1 cent, and roughly 85% of individuals were 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis of the entire Danish population's savings responses to active-choice subsidies versus passive automatic-contribution policies.
why_it_matters: Gives a large-sample, quantified answer to whether a default changes real amounts saved or just nominal enrolment; passive defaults produced genuine new savings while active-choice-style incentives mostly moved money around, arguing against assuming active choice alone captures the benefit.
limitations: Retirement/tax-advantaged accounts rather than a liquid consumer round-up product
Danish population and tax system, not an app context
No direct measurement of user-level withdrawal or disengagement over weeks/months
relevance_reason: The strongest available quantitative evidence on whether default/passive enrolment changes real saved amounts versus just reallocating them, directly bearing on the brief's amount-vs-nominal-enrolment question and the active-choice trade-off.

key_finding: Field experiments show that 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision with no default) and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option can motivate behavior change as an alternative or complement to automatic default enrollment.
methodology: abstract-only; series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against default/opt-out framing, drawing on the Carroll et al. active-choice literature.
why_it_matters: This is the origin paper for the 'active choice' design option itself, and its 'enhanced active choice' variant is a concrete, testable middle design between opt-in and opt-out for the enrolment decision.
limitations: Original application is medication adherence, not financial products, so effect sizes may not transfer directly
Abstract gives no quantified effect sizes
Highlighting losses to steer choice itself raises the dark-pattern questions the brief wants us to watch for
relevance_reason: Directly proposes and tests the active-choice and enhanced-active-choice mechanisms the brief is deciding between as an entry design, making it foundational to that specific choice.

key_finding: This NBER review chapter synthesises household-finance behavioural regularities and surveys firm/government interventions, including choice architecture, defaults, product design and disclosure, used to shape household financial outcomes.
methodology: Narrative review/synthesis chapter covering consumption/savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, and behavioural interventions across each.
why_it_matters: Provides a broad synthesis of which choice-architecture levers, including defaults, work in household finance generally, giving the project a framework to weigh the round-up feature's design against the wider evidence base rather than a single study's estimate.
limitations: Narrative overview, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
Covers many domains beyond enrolment defaults specifically
Substantial retirement-plan content that does not carry the consumer-app mechanism
relevance_reason: The synthesis/review the brief asks for, situating the enrolment-default decision within the broader behavioural household-finance evidence base.

key_finding: At three large firms, automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and default conservative fund, and half still held the default rate and fund after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing 401(k) contribution and investment choices before/after automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: Directly answers whether a pre-set level anchors the choice people end up making, since half of participants were still anchored on the default years later, exactly the risk in shipping a pre-selected round-up multiplier rather than a blank field.
limitations: 401(k) employer retirement plan, the mechanism the brief says does not carry over
Predates app-based, liquid, self-directed consumer products
Persistence measured at 3 years for retirement contributions, not weeks/months of liquid round-up saving
relevance_reason: The clearest direct precedent for anchoring on a pre-set contribution level, with multi-year persistence data, exactly the second design decision (preset multiplier vs blank field) the brief is deciding.

key_finding: In a randomized experiment on salary-linked savings accounts in Afghanistan, default enrollment increased participation by 40 percentage points, equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and it also increased subsequent active saving after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment assigning employees to different default variants of a salary-linked savings account, plus follow-on interventions isolating mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Gives a precise, causally-identified default effect size and shows the mechanism (present bias, cognitive cost) behind it, speaking directly to whether an opt-out round-up default is helpful scaffolding or an exploitation of decision-avoidance the EU dark-pattern lens would flag.
limitations: Salary-linked account set up by an employer, not a self-initiated consumer banking app feature
Afghan labour-market context differs sharply from an EU digital-banking population
No multi-month withdrawal/disengagement tracking reported in the abstract
relevance_reason: The most rigorous causal estimate of default-effect size and its psychological mechanism, informing both the effect-size question and the manipulation-risk question the brief raises.

key_finding: A randomized reminder nudge for credit card payments cut late fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Field experiment (RCT) with a financial management platform in Brazil, randomizing payment reminders and measuring downstream fee outcomes across account types.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's concern that a nudge or default can work well on average while harming a specific subgroup — here overdraft-prone users are made worse off — which is exactly the distributional risk the round-up feature needs to check before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: studies reminder nudges, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level presets
credit card/overdraft context in Brazil, not a EU round-up savings product
no measurement of persistence beyond the experiment window
relevance_reason: Provides a rigorous, quantified counter-example to 'nudges/defaults always help', showing concentrated harm in a vulnerable subgroup, which speaks to C5 (distributional and manipulation risk) even though the intervention type differs from an enrolment default.
